body: Rome. Yossarian returns to the apartment building where the squadron's officers used to stay. The rooms have been emptied. The girls are gone. Only an old woman is sitting there.

He asks what happened. Soldiers came, she says, wearing white helmets and carrying clubs. The girls cried and asked whether they had done anything wrong. No. Then why were they being driven out? Catch-22. By what right? Catch-22.
Yossarian asks whether the soldiers showed them the regulation.
The old woman says they did not have to show it. The law said they did not have to.
Which law said that?
Catch-22.

This conversation comes near the end of the book. Near the beginning, the same name means something else. Doc Daneeka explains that an insane airman can be grounded, but must request it himself. Concern for one's safety in the face of a real and immediate danger is evidence of sanity. A sane man has to keep flying. Yossarian whistles at the neatness of it.

Placed side by side, these are not the same rule. The doctor's version is a logical circle: premise and conclusion bite each other's tails. You can diagram it, even admire it, as Yossarian does. The Roman version contains no such logic. It means that they are entitled to do whatever we cannot stop them doing. One is an ingenious trap. The other is a statement of fact.

They share a name, but not because they share a content. **The name does not regulate anything. It makes the question “By what right?” impossible to pursue.** The girls ask for a reason; the soldiers supply a word. Once it has been spoken, questioning is over. All that remains is moving belongings and shutting doors.

Yossarian wants to see the text of the regulation. Here at last someone asks for it. He does not see it, and neither has anyone else. There is no text, no numbered provision anyone can produce, no date of enactment, no author anyone can point to.
The same shape returns throughout the book in different guises.

Clevinger is brought before the Action Board on charges that include breaking ranks, assault, misconduct, loitering, treason, provocation, cleverness, and listening to classical music. The verdict has effectively been reached before the hearing begins. He is accused of everything he has done and everything he has not done. How does he plead?

**His judges have decided that he is guilty, and their decision is the whole of their evidence.** Clevinger believes in reason more firmly than anyone in the squadron. He has prepared a defense. None of it finds a use. He never quite understands what has happened.

Captain Black launches his loyalty-oath campaign. An oath for a map, another for flying equipment, another before a meal, followed by the national anthem. The oaths multiply and the queues lengthen. No one can say that this is wrong: opposition to a loyalty oath is itself almost unsayable. Then Major de Coverley enters the mess hall and demands food, and the campaign stops. **No authority had needed to order it into existence; no formal order is needed to end it.**

In the hospital lies a soldier wrapped from head to foot in bandages, the soldier in white. One tube runs from his elbow to a bottle; another runs from his groin to a second bottle. When the upper bottle empties and the lower one fills, the nurses exchange them.

The men in the ward argue about whether anybody is inside. Nobody has seen his face. He has neither spoken nor moved. Later another completely bandaged soldier arrives. Dunbar insists that it is the same one. There is no way to prove or disprove it, and the difference makes no difference to the ward's routine.

The bottles continue to change places. The nurses continue to make their entries. The days pass. If something occupies the position, the process is working. Whether it is the same person, or whether there is a person there at all, is not a question the process has to answer.

Doc Daneeka fears death and never flies. To qualify him for flight pay, McWatt enters his name in the flight records each month. On the day McWatt crashes into a mountain, Daneeka's name is on the list. So Daneeka is dead. He stands in the squadron area while the news is read. He speaks; nobody answers. His wife receives the notification in America and eventually moves away.

A dead man lives in Yossarian's tent, as everyone calls him. His name was Mudd. On the day he arrived, before he had properly put down his luggage, he was sent on a mission and killed over Orvieto. His paperwork was incomplete; he was not on the roster. Not being on the roster, he had never arrived. Nobody can remove his possessions: to remove something, one must first acknowledge that it is there.

The chaplain is summoned for interrogation. What is he accused of? That, his interrogators explain, is what they mean to find out. They show him a signed document and ask him to account for it. He cannot. Exactly, they say.

The required number of missions was once twenty-five. Under Colonel Cathcart it becomes thirty, then thirty-five, forty, forty-five, fifty, fifty-five, sixty. It goes on climbing through sixty-five and seventy. Eventually it reaches eighty.

Cathcart raises the number because he wants to become a general and appear in the Saturday Evening Post. His ambitions are clear to the reader. **But the men in the aircraft have no access to the decision as he makes it, and no way to make his private ambition count as an answer.** From their seats, “the war requires another mission” and “a colonel wants his photograph in a magazine” have the same practical meaning: takeoff at five tomorrow morning.

That is what the regulation does. **It is less a chain fastening people down than a membrane between motive and execution.** Above it, someone has his reasons. Below it, someone has his assignment. Anything can fill the space between them, or nothing can, and the aircraft will still take off. Both sides of the membrane function normally. Nobody has neglected his job.
That is why it needs no author. Cathcart did not invent it. Neither did Korn. Generals Dreedle and Peckem, busy fighting each other, did not invent it either.

It grows where several individually defensible sets of rules meet. The flight-pay rule is in order. The death-notification rule is in order. So is the reporting-in procedure. Each component is legitimate, explicable, traceable to someone who once wrote it.

**What has no author has no single person with the authority to cancel it.** Every escape Yossarian tries is addressed to somebody or something specific: appeal to Major Major, appeal to Daneeka, shift the bomb line on a map, claim liver trouble and enter the hospital. Sometimes these devices work, for a day or two. The name belongs to nobody. There is nobody with whom to negotiate it, reason it away, or plead for mercy.
The old woman says that all the girls were driven out. She alone was left, because she was too old for the men to bother with.
It is not yet light when Yossarian leaves the building. He has not found the person he came to find: Nately's girl's twelve-year-old sister, somewhere on the streets of Rome.

He returns to Pianosa. The squadron eats much better than it did at the start of the war. There are fresh eggs, and goods brought from Malta. The man responsible for that has never lost a day's peace over this regulation.

body: Milo Minderbinder signs a contract with the Germans to bomb his own squadron with his own aircraft and his own pilots. The price is cost plus six percent.

The aircraft take off from their own runway and, as contracted, bomb the fuel stores, ammunition, hangars, and runway. Their own men are killed and wounded. Afterwards people demand an accounting. Milo opens his books and shows how much the syndicate has earned.
Then the matter passes, because everybody has a share.

Before he opens the books, he is close to ruin. The squadron curses him; his superiors threaten an investigation. He does not defend his motives or say that he was forced. He displays the figures and lets each person see what stands to his name.

He does not suppress the scandal through power or settle it through personal connections. He produces an account everybody can understand and everybody appears in. One by one, the people cursing him fall quiet. They have not been persuaded. They have found themselves on the page.
To see Milo clearly, we must first give him his full due. He is not merely a parasite.

Before he became mess officer, the squadron ate canned food. Afterwards it had fresh eggs. He travels the Mediterranean for them: buying in Sicily for a cent, selling in Malta for four and a half cents, buying back at seven, selling to the mess halls for five. Each egg seems to lose two cents, yet the syndicate profits, because he is the person at each stage of the transaction.

His position extends well beyond the squadron. He is mayor of Palermo, vice-governor of Malta, a potentate in Oran, caliph of Baghdad, even a rain god in parts of Africa. Crowds welcome his aircraft with drums and flowers. Their welcome is not simply the result of deception. He really does sell what they want to sell and bring in what they want to buy.

He keeps his contracts and takes his promises seriously. Nor is he cynical. He is, on the contrary, among the most earnest people in the book. When someone fails to understand the syndicate, he blushes, feels hurt, and patiently explains again. **What sets the machinery moving is not cynicism but a man's sincere belief.**

The bridge at Orvieto makes the point more clearly. Cathcart employs Milo to bomb it; the Germans employ him to defend it with antiaircraft guns. He accepts both contracts and both payments. The terms are openly negotiated and the accounts settled. On the day of the raid, he is on the ground directing the guns. The bridge is hit and aircraft are brought down. Each contract can report a job well done.

**He need not choose a side: in his accounts, both sides are opposite ends of one transaction.** Betrayal would require that one side first count as his own. He has classified neither side as his people and neither as the enemy. His ledger has no such columns.

Measured by fidelity to oneself, Milo fares remarkably well. He has something entirely his own, neither inherited from someone else nor adopted to win approval. He makes his rules and lives by them. Cathcart lives for other people's eyes, Korn for advancement, the generals for defeating one another. Milo lives for a system he considers his own.
**The trouble is not that he has no law of his own. It is that his law leaves no room for anybody else's.**
“Everybody has a share” sounds like recognition. It includes everyone, without exception. And it has real substance: the accounts, dividends, and eggs are real.

But the way it includes everyone is by converting each person into a shareholding. **A share is a form that can be entered in a ledger. Much of what belongs to a person cannot.** Once someone is a shareholder, whether he fears death, wants to go home, or has other plans does not appear in this account. Only the size of his holding does.

The slogan therefore works in two directions. In one direction it is true: everyone receives a distribution; no one is omitted or discriminated against. In the other, it has redefined “everybody” as something capable of holding a share.

Milo cannot see the difference, not merely because he refuses to look. His method is complete. It omits nothing it can calculate and leaves not even a space for what it cannot. If a ledger has no column for “not calculable,” the incalculable amounts to nothing within that ledger.

The squadron's anger does not last. To sustain an accusation against him would require an error that his accounts can recognize. The men who cursed him continue eating the food he brings and receiving the money he distributes.

The method hits a wall with Egyptian cotton. Milo buys the whole crop and cannot sell it. The syndicate faces collapse. His solution is to coat cotton with chocolate and distribute it as a snack. Someone tries it and spits it out.

His response matters. He sees nothing wrong with the idea. Whether cotton can be eaten does not enter as an independent question. It is merchandise; merchandise must be sold; unsold merchandise means a loss; a loss requires a remedy. He sincerely fails to understand the anger.

In eleven months, Milo has flown five missions, or four if one discounts the occasion when he was in the control tower. He generously excludes Orvieto, where he was on the ground directing the guns. Later he asks Cathcart for more missions. Bewildered by the syndicate's reasoning, Cathcart decides that others should fly for Milo and that Milo should receive the credit. To provide enough missions, the total requirement rises to eighty.

**The missions other men fly go under Milo's name; the increased requirement falls on everybody.** The arrangement slips into the book without a quarrel or a demand for an explanation. On an emergency mission after the increase, two aircraft collide. Dobbs and Nately die.
The squadron's life jackets contain carbon-dioxide cylinders for inflation. Milo removes the cylinders and sells them. When Orr's aircraft goes into the sea, the jackets will not inflate.

There should be twelve syrettes of morphine in the first-aid kit. When Yossarian searches it in the rear of the aircraft, they are gone. In their place is a neatly written note declaring that what benefits M&M Enterprises benefits the country. Milo Minderbinder has signed it.
Yossarian has only two aspirin tablets left. He brings them to Snowden's mouth. Snowden's bloodless lips cannot take them.

The note is the nearest Milo comes to this moment. He is not there and will never know it happened. In his accounts the morphine is inventory, with a price and a destination. The calculation contains no internal mistake. **It simply never asks whom those supplies were originally meant for.**

At one point the book places the two things directly together. On the day of Snowden's burial, Yossarian sits naked in a tree, looking down. Milo climbs up beside him with a piece of chocolate-covered cotton and asks him to taste it. One bite, he insists, will show how good it is.
Below them, earth is being put into the grave. Milo does not look down, nor think to look. He is working out another account. That account is perfectly clear to him. Every step follows from the last.

body: When Yossarian crawls to the rear of the aircraft, Snowden is lying on the floor. There is a hole in his outer thigh, roughly the size of a hand. The muscle inside is still moving.

Yossarian first reaches into the kit for morphine. It is missing. He finds sulfanilamide. He applies a tourniquet, carefully, because this is something he knows how to do. He dusts the wound, covers it with gauze, wraps the bandage round and round, and tucks in the end. Nothing in this sequence is wrongly done.
When he finishes, he feels relieved. The blood is clotting. Snowden will live, he thinks, if they can just get him back to the ground.
Then Snowden says that he is cold.
Yossarian says, “There, there.” He does not know what else to say.
Snowden says again that he is cold.
Yossarian opens his flak suit.
Snowden's entrails spill onto the floor towards Yossarian's feet. There is another wound. A fragment has entered from the other side, where the clothing has kept the damage covered.

All this time Yossarian has been correctly treating a wound that is not the fatal one. Every action is proper. His judgment rests on what he can see, and what he can see has been selected by a piece of clothing. This is not simply incompetence. A calmer, more skilled, better-trained man could perform the same sequence, so long as he did not first open the flak suit.

The jokes across the first forty chapters have this shape: Major Major's name, the loyalty oaths, Daneeka's death notice, Milo's ledger. Their absurdity lies in how impeccably they are processed. The procedure is sound; no individual dereliction explains it. They are treating the wrong place. **The comic machinery of the first forty chapters is the wound in Snowden's thigh.**
After Snowden dies, Yossarian thinks of man as matter: dropped, he falls; set alight, he burns; buried, he rots like refuse. Without the spirit, a human being becomes waste.
It looks like a complete reduction, a person counted as so much material. It is indeed what Yossarian thinks at that moment. The book offers no cushioning around it.
Yet the book's structure is doing something else.

Snowden dies over Avignon before the story's opening. Across forty-two chapters, the scene returns again and again, each time disclosing a little more. At first there is the complaint of cold. Later come the rear of the aircraft, the hole, the tourniquet, the sulfanilamide. Then the helpless reassurance. What lies under the flak suit is withheld until Chapter 41, the penultimate chapter.
**If a person were only a quantity of matter, this scene would not need to be told so many times.**

An event is repeated, approached a little more closely each time, and not completed until near the end. The telling keeps circling something. Not the entrails: those can be described, and Heller describes them minutely with ordinary comparisons, matches and toothpicks and tomatoes. **What the narrative circles has no ready name and no ready place to go.**

This form puts the reader in the same position. Early on, we know that a man named Snowden has died. Later we know that he died in the rear of an aircraft and someone dressed his wound. We think we know what happened, just as Yossarian thinks he has dealt with the injury. When the penultimate chapter opens the clothing, more than the clothing is opened.

A novel that rearranges time could have given us the whole scene anywhere. Heller does not. He distributes its fragments through the forty-two chapters. At intervals we encounter it again, knowing a little more and still not enough.

In an early chapter, Yossarian asks a question at an educational session. Other men ask disruptive questions about who Spain is or why Hitler is. Yossarian asks where the Snowdens of yesteryear are. When he is not understood, he tries it in French. The room becomes displeased.

It is not merely the wordplay that troubles them. **The question has a definite answer, and the room knows it.** Snowden died over Avignon. The question turns that event into a formula suitable for disrupting a lecture, yet each repetition also brings the event into the room.

All Yossarian can say beside Snowden is his little phrase of reassurance. It is hardly consolation. Consolation offers something in exchange for what has been lost. These words contain nothing. They are the sound a person makes when there is nothing to say. Elsewhere Yossarian is wonderfully quick with words, quoting regulations, tangling an officer in arguments, talking an entire ward into changing its account. At the rear of the aircraft he has only this phrase, repeated.
From that day he wants one thing: to live. Accurate bombing matters less than pulling away as soon as the bombs are released. He pretends to be ill, moves the bomb line on the map, refuses to fly.
The system does have a category for wanting to stay alive.

It calls it cowardice. **The trouble is not that there is nowhere to put the desire. There is somewhere, and once entered there it cannot get out.** Cathcart sees a nuisance, Korn a threat to morale, Danby a failure to appreciate the larger picture. A man who has seen beneath the flak suit can occupy only that box on their form.

Others devise their own methods. Hungry Joe screams through nightmares after completing his missions, while he waits to go home; a new assignment lets him sleep. Dunbar seeks boredom because it lengthens time and therefore life. Later he is “disappeared”; a nurse hears the term behind a door, and nobody can explain it. **Each response has its own sense. None has a name on the form.**
Yossarian receives his medal for Ferrara naked, standing in formation and embarrassing Cathcart in front of General Dreedle. Cathcart stores it among the grievances he keeps against him.
The book gives a reason: Snowden's blood has soaked Yossarian's uniform. He cannot bear to put it on again.
Nobody in the squadron asks about that reason. They see a naked captain.

The book tells us almost nothing about Snowden before that day. His age, home, family, earlier work: none is supplied. He first appears already lying in the aircraft, and whenever he appears again, he is still there.

He has a surname, and that surname becomes a phrase with which to interrupt an educational session. Seen another way, when a person has been reduced to a name, the name catches in everyone's throat. Nobody can get it out smoothly.
Yossarian accomplishes nothing for him. The tourniquet, the powder, the words do not alter the outcome. The one thing he does accomplish is to remember the whole sequence, without dropping a step.
Snowden says that he is cold, and says it again. After the repetition, Yossarian reaches for the fastenings of the flak suit.

body: Aarfy stands at the window looking down. A crowd has gathered on the pavement. Michaela lies in its center. She is the maid who works in the building. Twenty minutes earlier she was cleaning a room.
Yossarian asks what he has done. Aarfy tells him. He raped her, then threw her from the window because she cried out and might be heard.
Yossarian tells him that he has killed someone and will be hanged.
Aarfy is untroubled. He smiles. Nobody will do anything to him. She was only a maid, he says. He adds that he has never paid for sex in his life.
A siren sounds below. Boots draw closer on the stairs, one flight after another. Yossarian says they are coming. Aarfy listens and leisurely straightens his clothes.
The military police enter, salute Aarfy, and apologize for the intrusion. Then they arrest Yossarian for being in Rome without a pass.

The two policemen do not need to understand themselves as villains. They have been trained to handle a specific problem: an officer where he should not be, unable to produce the required paper. They handle that problem correctly. From entry to arrest, nothing departs from their procedure. Their report can be entirely accurate.

The body is on the pavement. Calling it merely ignored would assume that it has first become visible as something that belongs within their remit. **In the job they have come to perform, what lies on the pavement does not become a case they must handle.** They pass it, go upstairs, complete the task, and come down again.

Aarfy's sentence is harder still to confront. “Only a maid” is not an empty space. It is a whole account of the world. An empty space is passive and local. **An account can be spoken, accepted, and carried elsewhere.** Aarfy is not improvising a defense. He states something he considers long established, without even adopting the tone of a man who must justify himself.
Yossarian is taken back to Pianosa. Cathcart and Korn say they have found a solution for him. Korn says they have considered it for a long time, and smiles.

The terms are these: Yossarian goes home, becomes a major, receives another medal, and returns as a hero. In exchange he will speak well of them, to reporters, to his family, to the soldiers who come after him.
Is that all, Yossarian asks?
Korn wants him to like them, join them, become their friend, become one of them.

Korn himself calls the arrangement despicable and disgusting. He hides nothing. He describes its baseness while predicting Yossarian's acceptance. For him there is no contradiction: an arrangement's being vile and its being workable are separate questions.
They are not buying silence. They have cheaper and quicker ways to obtain that: transfer him, confine him, court-martial him. They go to this trouble because silence is insufficient.

**They are buying not a sentence but a person who can say it.** Praise would be worthless if everyone knew what Yossarian really thought. What has value is his becoming the sort of person from whom those words can issue without resistance.
And Yossarian agrees.
This must be seen plainly: he does not refuse on the spot. He agrees. Korn tells him to use their familiar names, Blackie and Chuck. When he leaves the office, the arrangement has been made.

Earlier he refused a less demanding offer: fly only safe missions until he reaches the required total. He rejected it because somebody would still have to fly the dangerous ones. If not he, then someone else.

Major Danby makes the best defense of the system in the book. He is not wicked, nor personally enriched by it. He serves his country, he says. Cathcart and Korn are his superiors. Obedience is the contribution he can make to the war.
Yossarian tells him that his country no longer needs this service. The people he is helping now are Cathcart and Korn.
Danby says he tries not to think about that. He concentrates on the larger result, forgets that they are also succeeding, and pretends that they do not matter.
This is not merely sophistry. It is an honest man's honest admission. It is also a reason the system can keep working.
By then Orr is missing. His aircraft went down at sea and he was not found. The squadron has regarded him as its greatest fool, repeatedly shot down yet continuing to fly without apparent fear.
Then word comes that he has reached Sweden in a dinghy.

Everything changes its meaning. The repeated descents were practice, not simply bad luck. His success in losing none of his crew was part of that practice. The comfortable tent was something he could leave behind for another man. Again and again he invited Yossarian to fly with him. Yossarian always refused: flying with Orr seemed too dangerous.
**The way out had been there all along, looking exactly like incompetence.**

Yossarian's final departure needs two things at once. First, somewhere to stand: Sweden is no longer an idea but a route someone has traveled from this island. Second, people who treat him as a person. Danby presses a thick bundle of Italian money into his hands and holds them in both of his own. The chaplain rushes in with clothes in a pillowcase. Yossarian should run; he will stay and challenge Cathcart and Korn whenever he sees them.

**With a route but no people, Yossarian is still in the office learning to say Blackie. With people but no route, they can only stay on the island together.** Danby, the best defender of the system, is also the man who gives him the money. He has not refuted all his earlier words. He has done something else as well.

Danby calls it running away from responsibility. Yossarian says he is running towards responsibility. Saving his life by escaping the island is not a negative act; the real evasion belongs to those who stay and continue flying. This is his account of his decision. The book neither certifies it nor takes it apart.

The chaplain stays. He will harass Cathcart and Korn whenever he meets them, and even challenge General Dreedle. Yossarian reminds him that Peckem has replaced Dreedle. Then Peckem, the chaplain says.
They choose opposite directions, one leaving and one staying, in the same hospital room within minutes of each other. **The book does not rank one above the other.**
Yossarian runs out. Nately's girl is waiting outside with a knife. The blade comes down; he avoids it by inches and runs.
The last sentence holds the knife and the running together.

The person holding the knife is not Cathcart, Korn, or Aarfy. It is a girl whose name the book never gives, because Nately is dead. He died on the emergency mission after the requirement rose to eighty, when Dobbs swerved to avoid flak and collided with his aircraft. Nobody takes responsibility. She cannot find the responsible person, so she attacks the man who brought the news.

The person most determined to find someone answerable for a particular death has chosen the wrong man. Around the other deaths, from Snowden to Michaela, that search for an accountable person has scarcely begun.
